messages.subject: Erratic results from secr.fit
messages.body_plain:
I came across an issue when responding to a question on phidot that should be known more widely. Valeria Boron asked why estimates from a 74-day binary 'proximity' dataset changed when the data were collapsed to single-occasion binomial count data. Theoretically they should not change (Efford, Dawson & Borchers 2009).

The problem was numerical (meaning, you can blame the programmer if you like). Essentially, model fits can be sensitive to the setting of the details argument 'minprob' in secr.fit. Set this to a small enough value and the estimates become stable. For example
[code]secr.fit(CH, ..., details = list(minprob = 1e-200))[/code]
seems OK, and in future versions I'll make that the default instead of 1e-50. It is possible that this may have affected other people's analyses. Always cross check your results! In this case I used some simple R code that calculated the likelihood quite independently of secr.fit(), and I'll look at ways to make that available.

The data collapsed to a single occasion gave the correct answer and the original analysis was wrong.  I suspect it is a problem only with 'extreme' datasets (few animals, many occasions, and possibly poor model fit due to unmodelled camera site effects).

(Incidentally: the likelihoods differ by a constant (the sum of binomial coefficients for each animal x site count) that depends on the data but not the parameter values; certainly the original and collapsed models should not be compared by AIC).

Murray

messages.subject: Analyzing data from clustered camera traps with spatial mark-resight models
messages.subject_clean: Analyzing data from clustered camera traps with spatial mark-resight models
messages.body_plain: I am writing to get feedback on whether a clustered design for cameras rather than a uniform grid poses any problems in analysis of data with spatial mark-resight models models. Can anyone provide me with insights on this?   I am considering a clustered design (for a study of cats) because this appears to be more feasible logistically than a uniform grid and also may allow me to place more cameras in better locations (i.e., where there is a higher probability of obtaining photographs).  Thanks for any help.

messages.subject: Re: Analyzing data from clustered camera traps with spatial mark-resight models
messages.subject_clean: Analyzing data from clustered camera traps with spatial mark-resight models
messages.body_plain:
The ability to cluster detectors or otherwise deviate from traditional grid patterns is one of the benefits of using spatially explicit capture recapture. However, it does not free you from general requirements of spatial sampling: if you only sample high-density patches of course your result will not apply to the landscape as a whole. You might consider stratifying your sampling; this requires a little extra (unpublished) post-analysis manipulation, but it's nothing to be afraid of.

Also note the distinction between mark-recapture (newly detected animals are marked when they are found) and mark-resight (after initial marking, new unmarked animals remain unmarked). Spatially explicit mark-resight is entirely feasible (see e.g. book by Royle et al.) but has not yet been fully implemented in software using maximum likelihood - it may be included in 'secr' later this year.

Murray
